{{For|a related alternating partial sum of factorials|Alternating factorial}}
{{More footnotes|date=January 2021}}
{{short description|Divergent series that can be summed by Borel summation}}
In mathematics, 
:<math>\sum_{k=0}^\infty (-1)^k  k!</math>
is a [[divergent series]], first considered by [[Leonhard Euler|Euler]], that sums the [[Factorial|factorials]] of the [[Natural number|natural numbers]] with alternating signs. Despite being divergent, it can be assigned a value of approximately 0.596347 by [[Borel summation]].

==Euler and Borel summation==
This series was first considered by [[Leonhard Euler|Euler]], who applied [[summability method]]s to assign a finite value to the series.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Euler |first=L. |author-link=Leonhard Euler |year=1760 |title=De seriebus divergentibus |trans-title=On divergent series |journal=Novi Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Petropolitanae |issue=5 |pages=205–237 |arxiv=1808.02841 |url=https://scholarlycommons.pacific.edu/euler-works/247/|bibcode=2018arXiv180802841E }}</ref> The series is a sum of [[factorial]]s that are alternately added or subtracted. One way to assign a value to this divergent series is by using [[Borel summation]], where one formally writes

:<math>\sum_{k=0}^\infty (-1)^k  k! = \sum_{k=0}^\infty (-1)^k \int_0^\infty x^k e^{-x} \, dx.</math>

If summation and integration are interchanged (ignoring that neither side converges), one obtains:

:<math>\sum_{k=0}^\infty (-1)^k  k! = \int_0^\infty \left[\sum_{k=0}^\infty (-x)^k \right]e^{-x} \, dx.</math>

The summation in the square brackets converges when <math>|x| < 1</math>, and for those values equals <math>\tfrac{1}{1+x}</math>. The [[analytic continuation]] of <math>\tfrac{1}{1+x}</math> to all positive real <math>x</math> leads to a convergent integral for the summation:

: <math>
\begin{align}
\sum_{k=0}^\infty (-1)^k k! & = \int_0^\infty \frac{e^{-x}}{1+x} \, dx \\[4pt]
& = e E_1 (1) \approx 0.596\,347\,362\,323\,194\,074\,341\,078\,499\,369\ldots
\end{align}
</math>

where ''E''<sub>1</sub>(''z'') is the [[exponential integral]]. This is by definition the [[Borel sum]] of the series, and is equal to the [[Gompertz constant]].

==Connection to differential equations==

Consider the coupled system of differential equations

:<math>\dot{x}(t) = x(t) - y(t),\qquad \dot{y}(t)=-y(t)^{2}</math>

where dots denote derivatives with respect to ''t''.

The solution with stable equilibrium at {{nowrap|1=(''x'',''y'') = (0,0)}} as ''t''&nbsp;→&nbsp;∞ has ''y''(''t'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;{{sfrac|1|''t''}}, and substituting it into the first equation gives a [[Power series solution of differential equations|formal series solution]]

:<math>x(t) = \sum^{\infty}_{n=1}(-1)^{n+1}\frac{(n-1)!}{t^{n}}</math>

Observe ''x''(1) is precisely Euler's series.

On the other hand, the system of differential equations has a solution

:<math>x(t) = e^{t}\int^{\infty}_{t}\frac{e^{-u}}{u}\,du.</math>

By successively [[Integration by parts|integrating by parts]], the formal power series is  recovered as an [[Asymptotic expansion|asymptotic approximation]] to this expression for ''x''(''t''). Euler argues (more or less) that since the formal series and the integral both describe the same solution to the differential equations, they should equal each other at <math>t=1</math>, giving

:<math> \sum^{\infty}_{n=1}(-1)^{n+1}(n-1)! = e\int^{\infty}_{1}\frac{e^{-u}}{u}\,du.</math>
